title: Pull the fields that matter
briefing: The scanner was the knock at the door. In `var/log/secure` someone with a password got in as `svc_backup`, a service account that has no business holding an interactive shell, and went straight to `sudo`.
Get the exact terminal and command from that `sudo` line. Copy them out with `cut`, not by eye: the same pipeline will run over ten thousand lines tomorrow.

lesson.p: `cut` slices each line into fields on ONE delimiter character and prints the fields you ask for. `tr` translates, squeezes, or deletes single characters as they stream through. Together they turn a log line into columns.

flags: split on commas, print field 2. The default delimiter is TAB, not space.
a list of fields / a range / field 3 to the end of the line
translate every comma into a newline: one field per line
squeeze each run of spaces into one, so space-aligned columns become single-space fields
delete carriage returns: converts Windows CRLF line endings to Unix LF
translate each of the three characters to a space and squeeze the runs: several delimiters become one
show invisible characters: `^M` is a carriage return, `$` marks the end of each line

lesson.note: `cut` never treats two spaces as one delimiter. Columns padded with spaces (sar, ps, ls -l) give empty fields, so `-f4` lands on nothing. Squeeze with `tr -s ' '` first.
`cut` and `tr` read standard input. `cut FILE` works, but `tr` takes no file name: write `tr -d '\r' < FILE`.

examples.title: Two fields from a web log

stages.why: Split on single spaces. In Apache's combined format, field 1 is the client IP and field 9 is the HTTP status.
First four lines only, enough to check the columns are the right ones.

examples.title: Number the columns of a CSV

stages.why: Each comma becomes a newline, so each column name sits on its own line.
Number the lines. Now you know `cut -d, -f6` is net_tx_bytes without counting commas.

examples.output:
1	timestamp
     2	host
     3	cpu
     4	mem
     5	disk_io
     6	net_tx_bytes

examples.title: Squeeze spaced columns before cutting
examples.command: grep ' all ' training/sar.txt | tr -s ' ' | cut -d' ' -f1,4 | head -3

stages.why: Keep the data rows; the header and the blank line have no ` all `.
sar pads columns with runs of spaces. Without the squeeze, `cut -d' ' -f1,4` prints the time and an empty field, because fields 2-4 are the gaps between spaces.
Now field 1 is the time and field 4 is %user (field 2 is AM/PM, field 3 is `all`).
The owner column, which is also the last one on each line.
Every line ends in `^M$`: a carriage return, then the newline. The file came from Windows, and the `\r` is now part of the last field.

examples.title: Strip them, and anchored matches work again

stages.why: `$` anchors at the end of the line, but the line ends in `\r`, so nothing matches: 0.
Delete every carriage return. `tr` reads standard input, hence the `<`.
The same pattern now finds the line: 1.

challenge.question: In var/log/secure, svc_backup ran exactly one command through sudo. On which terminal (the TTY= value), and what was the command (the COMMAND= value)?
challenge.format: The TTY value, one space, then the command, for example pts/9 /usr/bin/id

hints: Find the line first: `grep 'svc_backup : TTY' var/log/secure`. That is sudo's command record; the `pam_unix(sudo:session)` line next to it has no command.
The line mixes three separators: spaces, ` ; ` and `=`. `tr -s ' ;=' ' '` turns all of them into single spaces. Then count the fields and keep two with `cut -d' ' -f`.

debrief.alternative: grep 'svc_backup : TTY' var/log/secure | tr ';' '\n' | grep -E 'TTY=|COMMAND=' | cut -d= -f2 | tr '\n' ' '
why: `sudo /bin/bash` is the whole escalation: a root shell, after which sudo logs nothing else. Everything svc_backup did next was done as root, and only auditd (Level 8) still sees it.

A service account with a sudo rule that allows a shell is a classic finding. On RHEL, check `sudo -l -U svc_backup` and the files under `/etc/sudoers.d/`; a rule that names specific commands must never include a shell, an editor, or anything else that can start one.

The alternative turns each `;` into a newline, so the key=value pairs land on separate lines. That works for any key=value log, whatever order the keys come in. Counting fields is quicker, but breaks as soon as the line shape changes.
